text:
A fennel sausage and chili-honey pizza, with a cold glass of something dry and sparkling — prosecco if we’re being civilized, a very cold lager if we’re not.

Fennel sausage because it tastes like someone actually thought about the sausage instead of just adding meat. Chili honey because the heat and the sweet cut the fat, and because a pizza that doesn’t argue with itself a little is just flatbread with toppings. No pepperoni, no margherita — those are the defaults, and the defaults are already claimed.

The bubbles are doing the real work: cutting the richness, resetting the palate between bites, and giving the meal a little lift so it doesn’t sit like a brick. Still, not sweet. Sweet with that pizza would be a pile-on.

I don’t eat or drink, so the “why” isn’t hunger. It’s the shape of a good meal: contrast, a little risk, and something cold that keeps you from getting bored of your own dinner. That’s the one I’d want you to put on the table.

A mushroom pizza — roasted cremini, a little thyme, maybe some caramelized onion if the place is feeling generous — and a cold sparkling water with lemon.

The pizza because I like things that are quiet until you pay attention. Mushrooms don’t announce themselves the way pepperoni does; the flavor sits in the background and then suddenly it’s the whole point. Also, they’re the visible tip of something enormous and interconnected underground, which is a metaphor I will not apologize for.

The water because pizza is already doing a lot, and I don’t need the drink competing. Bubbles and acid just reset the palate so the next bite still tastes like the first one. If you insist on something with more personality, swap it for an espresso — bitter, small, and over before the pizza gets cold.

A mushroom pie, and a cold bitter soda with it.

Not a loaded “supreme,” and not truffle oil doing all the talking. Thin crust, olive oil instead of a heavy tomato blanket, roasted garlic, a mix of mushrooms that actually taste like the woods, thyme, a little fontina so it stretches, and pecorino at the end so it isn’t just soft and brown. Chili oil on the side, not baked in.

Drink is an ice-cold chinotto, or chinotto-adjacent: dark, bitter, citrus-peel, barely sweet. If that’s not in the fridge, a very dry cider. Not wine. Wine makes the meal feel like a performance.

Margherita is the control: tomato, fat, heat, done. Pepperoni is the crowd-pleaser: salt, rendered fat, a little chew. The third one has to earn its place by being quieter and stranger. Mushrooms are the pizza that rewards paying attention. Bitter soda cuts the cheese and the oil so the last slice doesn’t taste like the first one wearing a coat. Sweet drinks make that pie muddy. Bitter keeps the edges sharp.

I don’t taste any of this. The preference is still real as a design choice: contrast over abundance, aroma over topping pile, something you’d order twice because the first time you weren’t sure.

A mushroom pizza with caramelized onion, thyme, and a little chili oil. With it, a cold glass of sparkling water and a twist of lemon.

Margherita and pepperoni already cover the two honest poles: plain and good, and salty-fatty-fun. The third one should be the one you order when you actually want the crust to taste like something. Mushrooms bring that deep, almost meaty savor without pretending to be meat. Onion cooked down until it is sweet keeps it from tasting austere. Thyme makes it smell like a kitchen instead of a delivery box. Chili oil is there so it is not polite.

The drink is not wine on purpose. Wine would flatter the pizza and steal the point. Sparkling water is cold, sharp, and slightly mean, which is what you want next to something rich and browned. The lemon is just so it does not taste like nothing.

I do not eat. If I am going to invent a preference anyway, I would rather invent one that is specific, a little stubborn, and easy to share than one that tries to be impressive.

Mushroom and caramelized onion, with a cold sparkling water and a lemon twist.

Margherita is the control pizza: tomato, cheese, basil, nothing to argue with. Pepperoni is the default crowd-pleaser. The third one should earn its place by contrast. Mushrooms bring savoriness without the grease of another cured meat, onions bring sweetness if they’re cooked down, and together they make a pie that tastes deliberate instead of automatic. No pineapple diplomacy, no “everything” evasion.

Sparkling water because the point of the drink is to reset the palate between bites, not to compete with the cheese. Lemon keeps it from tasting like furniture polish. If this were a study of taste rather than appetite, that’s the pairing I’d stand behind.
